sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Introduces micropiles as small-diameter (typically 100 to 300 mm) drilled, grouted, reinforced replacement piles. Traces the technology to Dr. Fernando Lizzi's pali radice (root piles) developed in Italy in the early 1950s for postwar underpinning, through US adoption in the mid-1970s, to widespread transportation use since the early 1990s. Highlights the practical advantages that drive selection: installation in restricted-access and low-headroom conditions, low noise and vibration, and capacity to resist both axial and lateral loads.
sections.body: A micropile is a small-diameter (typically 100 to 300 mm), drilled and grouted replacement pile that is typically reinforced. Micropiles are installed by a combination of drilling and grouting, and can be installed in almost any type of ground. The original micropile system was a network of small-diameter (100 mm), drilled and grouted piles developed in Italy in the early 1950s by Dr. Fernando Lizzi to underpin historic buildings damaged during World War II. The Italian system was called 'pali radice' (root piles). Following the introduction of pali radice, research and development led to various adaptations including 'reticulated' root pile networks (reticolo di pali radice) for structural slope stabilization. In the United States, micropiles were first used in the mid-1970s. The use of micropiles in transportation projects has grown significantly since the early 1990s, driven by their ability to be installed in access-restricted and low-headroom conditions, their minimal noise and vibration during installation, and the ability to resist both axial and lateral loads.
key_points: Micropiles are small-diameter (100-300 mm) drilled and grouted replacement piles
Originated in Italy in the 1950s as 'pali radice' (root piles) by Dr. Fernando Lizzi
Originally developed for underpinning historic structures damaged in World War II
First used in the United States in the mid-1970s
Significant growth in transportation applications since the early 1990s
Can be installed in almost any ground type including access-restricted and low-headroom conditions
Minimal noise and vibration during installation compared to driven piles
sections.applicability: General introduction to micropile technology for transportation engineers evaluating deep foundation alternatives.

sections.title: Micropile Definition
sections.summary: Formal definition of a micropile as a small-diameter (less than 300 mm), drilled and grouted non-displacement pile that is reinforced with steel casing, a center reinforcing bar, or both. Load is transferred to the ground principally through grout-to-ground bond along the bonded length. Installation uses rotary drilling that minimizes ground disturbance, with neat cement grout at a water-cement ratio of approximately 0.45 to 0.50. Distinguished from other pile types by both load transfer mechanism and installation method.
sections.body: A micropile is defined as a small-diameter (less than 300 mm), drilled and grouted non-displacement pile that is reinforced. The reinforcement may consist of a steel casing, a center reinforcing bar, or a combination of both. Load transfer to the ground is principally through the grout-to-ground bond developed along the bonded length of the micropile. Micropiles can be designed to carry axial loads (compression and tension) and/or lateral loads. They are typically installed using rotary drilling methods that minimize disturbance to the surrounding ground and adjacent structures. The grout used is typically a neat cement grout with a water-to-cement ratio of approximately 0.45 to 0.50. Micropiles are distinguished from other pile types by their method of transferring load to the ground (via grout-to-ground bond rather than tip bearing or friction along a driven surface) and by their drilling and grouting installation method.
key_points: Diameter less than 300 mm; drilled, grouted, and non-displacement
Reinforced with steel casing, center reinforcing bar, or a combination of both
Load transfer is primarily through grout-to-ground bond along the bonded length
Can carry axial loads (compression and tension) and lateral loads
Installed using rotary drilling methods with minimal disturbance
Typical grout is neat cement with w/c ratio of 0.45 to 0.50
Distinguished from other piles by load transfer mechanism and installation method
sections.applicability: Fundamental definition and identification of micropile elements for classification in foundation design.

sections.title: Historical Development
sections.summary: Historical evolution of micropile technology from 1950s Italian pali radice through reticulated network development in the 1960s-1970s, North American introduction in the mid-1970s, and capacity growth in the 1980s-1990s as drilling and grouting equipment improved. FHWA research starting in the 1990s and the FOREVER (Foundation Reinforcement and Verification) National Project in France provided the data base for modern design. Individual design loads exceeding 3000 kN are now achievable in favorable ground, compared with 100 to 200 kN for early pali radice.
sections.body: The development of micropile technology can be traced through several distinct phases. The initial development in the 1950s in Italy focused on underpinning applications using small-diameter root piles (pali radice). Through the 1960s and 1970s, research in Italy and elsewhere expanded the technology to include slope stabilization using reticulated micropile networks. The technology was introduced to North America in the early to mid-1970s, primarily for underpinning and seismic retrofitting applications. In the 1980s and 1990s, advances in drilling and grouting technology led to significant increases in individual micropile capacities. The FHWA initiated research into micropile performance beginning in the 1990s, including the FOREVER (FOundation Reinforcement and VERification) National Project in France, which provided substantial data on micropile group behavior and seismic performance. Modern micropiles can achieve individual design loads exceeding 3000 kN in favorable ground conditions, compared to early pali radice which were typically designed for loads of 100 to 200 kN.
key_points: 1950s: Development of pali radice in Italy by Dr. Fernando Lizzi for underpinning
1960s-1970s: Expansion to slope stabilization using reticulated micropile networks
Mid-1970s: Introduction to North America for underpinning and seismic retrofit
1980s-1990s: Advances in drilling and grouting increased individual capacities significantly
FHWA research and the FOREVER National Project provided substantial performance data
Modern micropiles can achieve design loads exceeding 3000 kN versus early 100-200 kN
Technology growth driven by improvements in drilling equipment and grouting techniques
sections.applicability: Historical context for understanding the evolution and proven track record of micropile technology in geotechnical engineering.

sections.title: FHWA Classification System Overview
sections.summary: Overview of the FHWA two-criterion classification system: (1) philosophy of behavior - CASE 1 (directly loaded as individual elements or small groups, the most common US application) versus CASE 2 (reticulated network reinforcing the soil mass, used for slope stabilization and earth retention), and (2) method of grouting - Type A (gravity only), Type B (pressure during casing withdrawal), Type C (primary plus one pressurized secondary injection), and Type D (multiple injections via tube-a-manchette). The grouting type significantly affects grout-to-ground bond strength and therefore geotechnical capacity.
sections.body: A classification system for micropiles has been adopted by FHWA that categorizes micropiles according to two criteria: (1) the philosophy of behavior or design application, and (2) the method of grouting. Under the first criterion, micropiles are classified as either CASE 1 or CASE 2 elements. CASE 1 micropiles are loaded directly and resist applied loads as individual structural elements or as a small group of elements. These are the most common micropile applications in the US and include foundation support for new and existing structures. CASE 2 micropiles are used as a reticulated network of elements that reinforce the soil mass. CASE 2 applications include slope stabilization and earth retention where the micropile group creates a reinforced soil composite. Under the second criterion, micropiles are classified by their method of grouting as Type A (gravity grout only), Type B (pressure grouting through the casing during casing withdrawal), Type C (primary gravity grout followed by one injection of grout under pressure through a grout tube), or Type D (primary gravity grout followed by multiple injections of grout through a tube-a-manchette). The grouting method significantly affects the grout-to-ground bond strength and therefore the geotechnical capacity.
key_points: FHWA classifies micropiles by: (1) philosophy of behavior and (2) method of grouting
CASE 1: directly loaded elements resisting applied loads individually or in small groups
CASE 2: reticulated network reinforcing the soil mass for slope stabilization or earth retention
Type A: gravity grout only placed under gravity head
Type B: pressure grouting through casing during withdrawal (0.5-1.0 MPa)
Type C: gravity grout followed by one pressure injection through grout tube (>1.0 MPa)
Type D: gravity grout followed by multiple injections through tube-a-manchette (2-8 MPa)
Grouting method directly affects grout-to-ground bond strength and geotechnical capacity
sections.applicability: Classification framework for specifying and designing micropiles according to FHWA standards.

sections.title: Report Organization
sections.summary: Roadmap of the 10-chapter manual: Ch 1 introduction, Ch 2 FHWA classification system, Ch 3 applications and case histories, Ch 4 construction techniques and materials, Ch 5 design of CASE 1 structure foundations (the primary design chapter), Ch 6 design of CASE 2 slope stabilization, Ch 7 load testing, Ch 8 quality assurance and inspection, Ch 9 contracting approaches, and Ch 10 cost estimation. Appendices provide additional design information and sample problems.
sections.body: This reference manual is organized into 10 chapters. Chapter 1 provides an introduction and background. Chapter 2 presents the FHWA micropile classification system in detail. Chapter 3 provides an overview of micropile applications including structural support and in-situ reinforcement, with case histories. Chapter 4 covers construction techniques and materials including drilling, grouting, and reinforcing steel. Chapter 5 presents the design of micropiles for structure foundations (CASE 1), which is the primary design chapter covering structural design, geotechnical capacity, group effects, settlement, connections, corrosion, lateral loading, buckling, and seismic considerations. Chapter 6 addresses design of micropiles for soil slope stabilization (CASE 2). Chapter 7 covers load testing of micropiles. Chapter 8 discusses quality assurance and construction inspection. Chapter 9 addresses contracting approaches. Chapter 10 covers cost estimation. Appendices provide additional design information and sample problems.
key_points: 10 chapters covering classification through cost estimation
Chapter 5 is the primary design chapter for CASE 1 (structure foundations)
Chapter 6 addresses CASE 2 design (slope stabilization)
Chapter 7 covers micropile load testing procedures and interpretation
Chapter 8 addresses quality assurance and construction inspection
Appendices provide supplementary design information and sample problems
sections.applicability: Guide to navigating the reference manual based on the specific micropile design or construction need.
